text: A sick donkey is the reason a man shoulders a wooden cross and walks it to the state capital. Zé's promise was made to Saint Bárbara in a language of exchange far older than any parish office: the animal lives, and he pays, on foot, in timber. Anselmo Duarte's film turns on what happens when a private bargain reaches a public door and has to be explained out loud — a faith that answers to saints meeting one that answers to doctrine, in daylight, in front of whoever happens to be standing around. Ninety-eight minutes, and very little of it is travel; the walking ends early and the hard distance is the last few metres. It took the Palme d'Or and the Academy's award for a film from abroad, and Brazilian critics have kept it among the hundred titles of their cinema.

The accident happens before the film starts; everything on screen after that is aftermath. A married woman tries to keep her shape while the town around her is rebuilt into something else, and the affair with her husband's friend arrives less like romance than like a hand reaching for a wall. Michelangelo Antonioni grants the industrial plant no villainy and no symbolism. It is simply the new arrangement of the world, and the question the film keeps circling is whether a nervous system can be brought to agree with it. Two hours at a tempo set by machinery rather than by people. Venice awarded it the Golden Lion, and it holds its place on the thousand-title list critics maintain, though what lasts is smaller and more physical than a list: the sense of a person one degree out of register with everything she touches.

A brother and a sister, wounded in ways neither will name, come back into each other's company after years apart. That is the whole of the plot, and John Cassavetes takes a hundred and forty-one minutes over it. The length is the argument. A shorter film would have to decide what these two are to each other and then illustrate it; this one stays in the room while the answer keeps changing, and lets scenes run well past the point at which a tidier picture would cut. What stands to be lost is not a relationship but an arrangement — two people who have organised their lives around a bond neither can live inside nor leave. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear, an unusual prize for a film in which nothing larger occurs than a homecoming and the long days after it.

Everyone in this film is acting on bad information, and none of them knows it. The owner of a small-town Texas bar learns that his wife is involved with one of his employees and arranges to have the problem removed; from there the picture works as a machine for converting each person's partial view of events into the next disaster. Ninety-seven minutes, a handful of people, one county. Joel Coen keeps the audience a fact or two ahead of everyone on screen, the oldest suspense arrangement there is, and at this temperature it produces a cold kind of laughter as well. The Sundance jury gave it their dramatic grand prize and the National Board of Review placed it in the year's ten. What holds up is the economy: no scene here is doing anything except setting a trap or springing one.

The embarrassment comes first: in this film a middle-aged accountant taking dance lessons is something to hide from his wife, his colleagues and himself. The hiding is what sets the plot moving — a woman glimpsed through a studio window, evenings unaccounted for, and in time a private detective hired by a wife who has noticed the perfume and the late arrivals home. Masayuki Suō gives the marriage its own investigation and takes her side of it seriously, which the premise never required. Two hours and sixteen minutes is a generous length for a comedy, and it is spent on the least romantic development available: the man discovers he likes dancing more than he likes the reason he began. Kinema Junpo and the Japan Academy both named it the year's best film.

A town whose old livelihood is failing decides that its way out is hula, performed by its own daughters. The plan is not a joke. Build a Hawaiian resort, staff the dancing with the young women of the households the dying trade supported, and sell the result to visitors. Sang-il Lee takes the arithmetic seriously: what it costs a place to turn its daughters into an attraction, and what the daughters get back, which turns out not to be nothing. The comedy runs on the incongruity of the scheme; the drama runs on everyone involved being short of options and knowing it. Japan sent it to the Academy that year and the Hōchi award named it best picture, with Kinema Junpo and the Japan Academy in agreement — a lot of institutional weight for a film about learning a dance that no one in town had ever needed.

Four years is a long time to leave a question unasked, and this man will not ask it directly. Released after a sentence for murder, he does not telephone his ex-wife; the arrangement is a handkerchief at the window, an answer he can read from the road without either of them having to speak. Yoji Yamada puts him in a car with two strangers and points it across Hokkaido, which makes the trip sociable and therefore harder — a hundred and nine minutes of company for someone who would rather not explain himself. What is at stake is not whether he can be forgiven. It is whether he can bear to go and find out. The comedy lives in the car, among people thrown together by chance; the weight lives at the far end of the road, in a window he has not seen in four years.

It begins in a painter's studio, with a portrait the artist would rather not discuss and a journalist who keeps asking. What he finally tells is the story of a young woman in Xochimilco, refused by her own village for what her mother was, and of the man who loves her and stands between her and everyone else. Emilio Fernández filmed it in 1944, and the frame around the story is not decoration: everything reaches the audience secondhand, through two men in a city discussing a woman who is not present to correct them. Cannes gave it the Palme d'Or, and Mexican critics have since counted it among the hundred films of their cinema. A hundred and two minutes, and the ache in it starts in that first scene — a life recounted by the man who painted it rather than by the woman who lived it.

The leverage is academic: a professor who can hold a diploma just out of reach decides the university sumo club needs another body. The graduating student he selects wanted nothing to do with it, and the teammates waiting for him have arrived by similarly poor logic — a club that must field a squad or be dissolved. Masayuki Suō finds his comedy in the gap between the sport's formality, a discipline with a rule for everything, and the amateurs now obliged to perform it. Then, somewhere inside the hundred and five minutes, the bouts begin to matter, and an audience that spent an hour laughing at these men is counting their wins. The Blue Ribbon jury named it the best picture of its year, a curious result for a comedy about undergraduates who were pressed into a ring.

A young man in Tokyo with no particular plan falls for a woman who is deaf and does not speak, and who works in a factory. Around that, quietly, the film conducts a family's arithmetic. His brother went to college; he did not, and the comparison sits in every room the two of them share, never said and never quite unsaid. Yoji Yamada films it in 1991 as ordinary domestic weather: nobody is cruel, and everybody keeps score. Two hours, and it is the father's opinion that organises all of them, whether or not he is in the room. What the son is after is not the girl or the job so much as an end to being the second answer to a question about the family. The courtship carries the tenderness — two people obliged to invent a way of talking, inside a family that has worn the usual one out.

A widow opens a summer house for the season, and the season turns out to be mostly visitors. She was an actress; she is now a woman receiving news, and much of the news concerns the dead. Kaneto Shindō builds the film out of those calls — old friends and acquaintances arriving with pieces of the past, each carrying a private reason for bringing it. The pace is a visitor's pace: arrival, conversation, departure, and then the house again. Nothing is raised in volume. What gives the hundred and ten minutes their weight is the profession she has set down, a life spent speaking lines other people wrote and now spent listening to other people's accounts of what happened. Kinema Junpo and the Japan Academy put it at the top of their year, and the Blue Ribbon jury named it best picture.

The whole operation exists because a visitor needs to sleep undisturbed. In 1997 the pope is coming to Rio de Janeiro, his lodging sits beside a favela the state does not control, and a captain of BOPE is ordered to quiet the area before the plane lands. José Padilha builds the film on that ratio: force applied, measured against the reason for applying it. The camera stays inside the unit rather than at a critical distance from it, which is the most consequential decision here — it hands over a vantage that is hard to hold and harder to refuse. A hundred and fifteen minutes at the tempo of a deployment. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear and Brazilian critics have kept it among the hundred films of their cinema: a picture with a very large audience and no comfortable seat anywhere in it.

Two days, one man, one hundred minutes, and no subplot to widen any of it. A businessman's trouble at work stops staying at work, and the film gives that collision a window short enough that nothing can be repaired by waiting. What stands to be lost is not the company but his ability to keep believing the account he gives of himself there. The Academy's award for best actor went to this performance, a fair index of where the weight sits: on speech, on a face, on the hours between one bad day and the next. John G. Avildsen holds the picture inside its two-day frame and lets a man talk himself toward a compromise at something close to real time. The writers' guild counted the screenplay among the year's original work, which fits a film built on how much a person can be brought to say aloud.

An affair needs a flat, a timetable and a plausible reason to be elsewhere; this is a comedy about the logistics. He is American, married, working in London. She is English and divorced. A week in Marbella is meant to settle what they are doing and instead complicates it, and back in London the two of them set about maintaining an arrangement neither had budgeted for. Melvin Frank keeps it to a hundred and six minutes and to the level of behaviour — the quarrels are about small practicalities and about who is being taken for granted — which is the only register in which the story stays funny rather than turning cruel, given the wife and children he has no intention of losing. The Academy's award for best actress went here, and the writers' guild counted the screenplay among the year's original work.
